newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China-ruled HK faces constitutional challenge.
newsitem.headline: China-ruled HK faces constitutional challenge.

text.p: Prominent Hong Kong lawyers challenged the legitimacy of the territory's China-appointed legislature on Wednesday, creating a potential constitutional crisis less than a month into Chinese rule.

The case took a twist when the government's top lawyer, defending the legislature, said the judges would be putting their own authority on the line if they ruled the Provisional Legislature was illegal.
Hong Kong's top judges were endorsed by the China-backed chamber shortly after it was sworn in following Britain's handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30.

Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa, now grappling with a host of problems from illegal immigrant children from mainland China and anger over his rolling back of civil freedoms and labour rights laws, said he was confident his government would win the case.
The landmark challenge, which calls into question the legitimacy of the Provisional Legislature and Hong Kong's entire legal system, arose from a criminal case.

Lawyers argued three people charged with criminal conspiracy should be set free because pre-handover laws under which they were charged ceased to be valid on July 1 when the China-backed chamber failed to formally adopt them, leaving a legal vacuum.

The challenge against the Provisional Legislature, formed under China's auspices in December, also strikes at the very heart of key Hong Kong institutions as the body has passed crucial laws governing the entry of migrants and labour rights.
Three heavyweight lawyers took over the case voluntarily on Wednesday for a face-off with the government's top lawyer.

Gladys Li, a stalwart of Hong Kong's British-based system of Common Law and one-time chairman of the Bar, and former pro-democracy legislator and lawyer Margaret Ng, joined forces with human rights lawyer Paul Harris for the showdown against Solicitor General Daniel Fung, heading the government team.

As the appeal court hearing reopened for its second day, Li said Hong Kong judges had the right to rule on the legality of the provisional chamber, which she argued did not find basis in the territory's mini-constitution, the Basic Law.
"If one looks for any warrant for the setting up of the Provisional Legislature, one does not find it here (in the Basic Law)," Li said.
"The Basic Law provides that the Hong Kong legislature must be constituted by elections. And here we have a body, the Provisional Legislature, which is in no sense an elected body."
But Fung argued the interim chamber was a creation of China's parliament, and was therefore, outside the purview of regional courts such as Hong Kong's.

"Regional courts have no more jurisdiction to question the acts of parliament, just like it was before the handover," Fung said. "Parliament is sovereign, parliament is supreme and once it has acted, it's not up to the courts to question."
"If the court should rule that the creation of the Provisional Legislature is illegal and unconstitutional, it will lead to absurdity," he told the court.
It would mean the authority of top judges, endorsed by the provisional chamber, could itself be challenged, Fung said.
But the case left Hong Kong's fledgling leader Tung unfazed.

"Am I surprised? No, I'm not surprised. Am I confident, I'm very confident. We'll win these cases. Will it rock the foundation of confidence? No, it wouldn't," Tung told reporters at a public function.
